title: The jinn listen
hook: a company of jinn listen to the Qur'an and say, be silent, and return to warn their people (46:29)

segments.voice: Yesterday: awzi'ni, the prayer at forty for gratitude, for me and my parents. Your line was inspire me to thank.

Somewhere outside Mecca, at night, a man is reciting the Qur'an. What he can't see is an audience gathering in the dark, listening so closely that they turn to each other and say: quiet. That's the scene in Surah Al-Ahqaf, near its end. The listeners are jinn. Popular culture has turned that word into the genie in a lamp. The Qur'an's jinn are something else entirely, and these ones begin by hushing each other.

Verse twenty-nine, in Pickthall's translation, describes a group of jinn turned toward the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, wishing to hear the Qur'an, and "when they were in its presence, said: Give ear!" Be silent, listen. When the recitation ended, they went back to their people as warners. The next verses give their speech: they've heard a book revealed after Musa, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and a straight road. So who are the jinn? The Qur'an says they were created from smokeless fire, and in Surah Al-Jinn they say of themselves that some among them are righteous and some are far from it. Surah Adh-Dhariyat, coming soon on this path, names jinn and humans together as the two kinds created to worship. The word comes from the root j-n-n, to hide or to cover. The same root gives janna, a garden thick enough to hide the ground, and janin, a child hidden in the womb. Jinn are, by their name, the hidden ones. Ibn Ishaq places this night on the Prophet's return from Ta'if, after the people there had driven him out with stones. Others connect it to a different night described in a hadith; the sources don't settle which, and that's fine to leave open. Some readers are struck by the timing in his account: at one of the lowest moments of his mission, rejected by people he could see, he was heard by listeners he couldn't. And the first thing they did was not argue. It was to hush each other.
screen: `GIVE EAR! THE JINN HUSH EACH OTHER.` · `MADE OF SMOKELESS FIRE, WITH CHOICE.` · `J-N-N: THE HIDDEN ONES.` · `HEARD AFTER TA'IF, BY UNSEEN LISTENERS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and, for a minute, just listen to what's in the room: hum, traffic, a bird, your breath, without naming any of it. Then, if you have a recitation you love, or any sacred text read aloud, give it your whole attention, the way those listeners did, doing nothing else at the same time.
Jinn. The hidden ones, made from smokeless fire, some righteous and some not, and in 46:29, an audience that hushed itself to listen. Today's word.
Your line: even the jinn listened. Before anything else, they hushed each other. That's day five hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to listen in silence when the Qur'an is recited, and many sit quietly through recitation at the mosque or at home; belief in the jinn as unseen beings with free will is part of mainstream Islamic teaching.

Yes; the Qur'an says they grant wishes to whoever finds them.

chat.meaning: The Qur'an says jinn were made from smokeless fire, and in 72:11 some are righteous and some not. Their name means the hidden ones.
